text: {"master_id": "howard-roberts", "work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "usage_notes": [{"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "equipment-setup", "narrative": "Use medium-heavy strings (.012 minimum first string) and medium-high action to build resistance that develops right-hand accuracy and left-hand strength. Narrow-gauge strings do not return to center fast enough to permit predictable accuracy. (Chapter 1, p. 3)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 1, p. 3: 'Extremely nar-row gauge strings do not create enough resistance or \"return\" to their center position quickly enough to permit the right hand to develope predictable accuracy, or to strengthen the left hand. So, use a medium-heavy set of strings; nothing smaller than an .012 first string, etc.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "equipment-setup", "narrative": "Use a medium-sized, medium-to-heavy celluloid pick. Avoid very large or oddly shaped picks. Pick thickness and material directly affect tone control and right-hand mechanics. (Chapter 1, p. 4)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 1, p. 4: 'Your pick should be of medium size, and medium to heavy in thickness. These externalize the method's three core feedback loops — time, self-monitoring, and session discipline. (Chapter 1, p. 4)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 1, p. 4: 'Also essential to the studies in this book will be: (1) a metronome, (2) a reel-to-reel or cassette tape recorder, and (3) an alarm clock or timer.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "intonation-verification", "narrative": "After setting up the guitar, verify that every note rings loud and clear across the entire fingerboard — like a grand piano. This is the primary diagnostic criterion for correct setup. (Chapter 1, p. 3)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 1, p. 3: 'After adjusting your guitar, make sure that each note rings loud and clear; just like a grand piano, over the entire range of the fingerboard.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "foundational-axiom", "narrative": "Speed is a byproduct of accuracy and is unattainable without it. Every practice decision — tempo targets, equipment choices, session structure — is downstream of this premise. Never chase speed at the expense of precision. (Chapter 1, p. 3)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 1, p. 3: 'Speed comes as a by-product of accuracy. Without accuracy, speed is unattainable.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "right-hand-mechanics", "narrative": "The right hand is the primary limiting factor for most modern guitar improvisers. Once a poor picking style becomes habitual it is extremely difficult to change — complete retraining is often required. Establish correct mechanics from the outset. (Chapter 2, p. 5)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The right hand seems to be the greatest limiting factor for most modern-day guitar improvisors. It appears that once a style of picking has become habitual, it is very difficult to change, and frequently, total retraining is required.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "right-hand-mechanics", "narrative": "Flexibility — the ability to adapt the right hand to a variety of moves — is the single governing principle of right-hand technique. Adaptability is more important than any fixed system. (Chapter 2, p. 5)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 5: 'flexibility-the ability to adapt the right hand to a variety of moves-is the key to longevity.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "right-hand-mechanics", "narrative": "Avoid any fixed anchor system — at the elbow, at the wrist, or grasping the pick-guard with the little finger. Such anchors may serve contextual sounds but create a hard speed ceiling when used as the foundation of overall right-hand technique. (Chapter 2, p. 5)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The big thing to avoid is any kind of anchor system that inhibits freedom of movement. Observe anchors at the elbow, at the wrist, grasping the pick-guard with the little finger, etc.; all of which may be functional for a specific sound, but should be viewed with caution when considered as the basis of an overall right hand technique.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "right-hand-mechanics", "narrative": "Keep the picking arm loose — any rigidness in the picking leverage system acts like a brick wall at fast tempos. Tension is a hard mechanical speed ceiling. (Chapter 2, p. 5)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 5: 'Keep it loose! - like a guy strumming a ukelele in a pineapple field. If the finger arrives first, two sounds result; if the pick arrives first, two sounds result. Perfect synchronization means a single audible attack. (Chapter 2, p. 5)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 5: 'Under any circumstances, the left and right hands must be in perfect synchronization. No Flams! If the finger attacks first and the pick follows, there will be two sounds instead of one. If the pick attacks first and the finger follows, again, two sounds instead of one.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "synchronization-diagnosis", "narrative": "To diagnose flams, play notes very slowly at all positions across the full fingerboard. Only slow play reveals the differential of attack. Fast warm-up playing obscures synchronization errors before they become ingrained. (Chapter 2, p. 5)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 5: 'To do so, play tones very slowly at all points on the fingerboard. Only in this way can we hear the flam effect. If we play fast in warming up, it becomes more difficult to hear the differential of attack.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "left-hand-mechanics", "narrative": "The left-hand thumb should ride along the approximate center of the back of the neck, enabling the perpendicular finger angle required for accuracy. (Chapter 2, p. 5)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The thumb of the left hand should ride along the approximate center of the back of the neck.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "left-hand-mechanics", "narrative": "Fret strings with fingers perpendicular to the fingerboard — straight up and down like piano hammers. Angling the finger moves the string from its center position, cutting accuracy and stretching the string out of tune. (Chapter 2, p. 5)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The fingers should operate straight up and down on the strings, like hammers in a piano, at a right angle to the fingerboard. Attacking the string at an angle will move the string from it's center position, both cutting down on accuracy and also stretching the string to sound out of tune.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "left-hand-mechanics", "narrative": "Lift fingers only high enough off the string to avoid noise when moving — not higher. Excess finger lift is wasted motion that reduces speed. Balance noise control against efficiency. (Chapter 2, p. 5)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The fingers should be lifted only high enough off the string to avoid string noise when moving, but not so high as to become wasted motion.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "left-hand-mechanics", "narrative": "Keep the left wrist fairly flat. Avoid severe arching, which produces undesirable strains and risks injury. A flat wrist posture supports both consistency and longevity. (Chapter 2, p. 5)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 2, p. 5: 'The wrist should maintain a fairly flat posture. Avoid severe arching of the left wrist as this can produce undesirable strains.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "fingerboard-navigation", "narrative": "Understand chord progressions through key centers — identify which major or minor scale the chords belong to by stacking thirds — rather than treating each chord independently. The dominant seventh chord uniquely identifies a single major key and is the most decisive harmonic landmark. (Chapter 3, pp. 6–7)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 6: 'When a given major or minor scale is stacked upon itself in thirds as shown in Example 1, it creates harmony characteristic of that scale.'"}, {"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 7: 'Eb 7 is a V chord (Dominant 7 type) which only appears once in any given major key, always as the V chord, and therefore, only one possibility, the V of Ab.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "fingerboard-navigation", "narrative": "When a new key center is reached in a progression, immediately move your hand to a convenient fingering pattern for that scale and improvise within that region of the guitar. Use the bracketed key centers as navigation instructions. (Chapter 3, p. 8)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 8: 'for each new one, move your hand to a convenient fingering pattern for that particular scale and do your improvising in that region of the guitar.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "fingerboard-navigation", "narrative": "Learn all five movable finger-per-fret scale patterns for any given key. Together they cover the entire fingerboard; mastering all five yields complete neck coverage. Tonics are circled in each pattern for visual targeting. (Chapter 3, pp. 8–9)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 8: 'There are five such patterns for any given scale. And each of these five are movable up or down the neck to the selected key or, they may be connected to increase the range.'"}, {"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 9: 'When these patterns are laid end to end, they cover the entire finger-board for any one key.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "fingerboard-navigation", "narrative": "Moving between the five scale patterns is achieved by exactly three techniques: (1) position skips, (2) stretching to the adjacent pattern, or (3) sliding on the half step between patterns. These three moves constitute the complete system for full-neck fluency. (Chapter 3, p. 10)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 10: 'There are essentially three \"moves\" involved in moving from one pattern to another. (1) Position skips ... (2) Stretching from one pattern to the next, ascending or descending; or (3) Sliding on the half steps.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "fingerboard-navigation", "narrative": "Prioritize developing a strong visual imprint of each pattern coupled with its sound. Specific fingerings within a pattern may change during improvisation — the visual/auditory internalization is the durable goal, not mechanical fingering adherence. (Chapter 3, p. 10)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 10: 'The most important thing here is to develop a strong visual imprint of the pattern itself, coupled with the tone sequence it produces (the sound) with the view that when improvising, the fingerings may be open to change at any time.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "fingerboard-navigation", "narrative": "The ultimate goal of key-center study is to play changes by ear rather than through intellectual calculation. Analytical key-center identification is the means; ear-based improvisation is the end. (Chapter 3, p. 8)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 8: 'the ability to play over changes by ear, can be viewed as the ideal end result.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "fingerboard-navigation", "narrative": "Play arpeggios within the scale pattern corresponding to the key center of the chord, not as isolated chord shapes. For example, a IIIm7–VIm7–IIm7–V7 progression in Bb means selecting one of the five Bb patterns and playing all arpeggios within it. (Chapter 3, p. 9)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 9: 'arpeggios will be easier to handle if they are played within a scale pattern that corresponds to the key center from which the chord is derived, e.g. the progression Dm7, Gm7, Cm7, F7 is a III, VI, II, V Progression in the key of Bb. Therefore, one would select one of the five patterns for that key and play the arpeggios in that pattern.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "line-construction", "narrative": "Common tones — notes shared between two or more consecutive chords — are a valid and deliberate relief technique. When playing non-stop eighth notes or triplets, the line does not need to keep moving; sustaining a common tone flattens the line and provides relief from excessive vertical movement. (Chapter 4, p. 11)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 11: 'A common tone is a note that is common to two or more chords, a very simple technique but not to be overlooked, i.e. when playing non-stop eighth notes, or triplets, etc., it is not necessary to keep the line moving at all times. The line can be flattened out --- a nice relief from excessive vertical movement.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "line-construction", "narrative": "Arpeggios outline bar harmony and provide a strong contrast to scale movement. They create smooth rolling lines at steeper melodic angles than scales, and should be used as a distinct color alongside scale passages. (Chapter 4, p. 13)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 13: 'Arpeggios are specifically chords, broken up into single notes. They are effective in outlining the bar harmony and offer a nice contrast to scale movement as they create smooth rolling lines, at sharper angles than scales.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "line-construction", "narrative": "Use interval skips to create sharp, dramatic lines that break up scale monotony. Large interval skips are a primary antidote to the beginner trap of playing exclusively scalar lines. (Chapter 4, p. 13)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 13: 'Interval skips create sharp, dramatic lines. An interval is the distance between any two notes. Large interval skips can be a valuable tool for creating interesting lines and can have a dramatic effect in breaking up the monotomy of excessive scale movement.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "line-construction", "narrative": "Derive all interval skips diatonically — respecting the scale's half steps — so that sequences of thirds, sevenths, ninths, etc. produce combinations of major and minor intervals rather than parallel intervals. Parallel interval sequences violate the key's internal structure and destroy tonality. (Chapter 4, p. 13)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 13: 'Any sequence of interval skips, 3rds, 7ths, 9ths, etc., can easily be applied to a key center by playing scale intervals that take into account the half steps of the scale, thus, resulting in combinations of major and minor 3rds or major and minor 7ths (not, parallel 3rds, 7ths, etc.)'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "line-construction", "narrative": "Do not play more than 3–4 consecutive scale tones in the same direction before changing direction or introducing a skip. Exceeding this limit produces lines that sound purely scale-like — the most common beginner flaw. Limiting stepwise runs forces interval skips and melodic variety. (Chapter 4, p. 13)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 13: 'A most common complaint of beginning improvisors is that their playing tends to become too scale-like. One solution to this could be to stop playing things that \"sound\" like scales, for example, as an exercise; don't play more than 3 or 4 scale tones in the same direction.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "scale-selection", "narrative": "Use the diminished scale (alternating whole steps and half steps, symmetrical) most commonly over dominant 7th chords or diminished chords. (Chapter 4, p. 12)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 12: 'The Diminished Scale (symetrical, consecutive whole step and half steps) most commonly used over dominant 7th chords or diminished chords.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "dominant7", "function_role": "scale-selection", "narrative": "The whole-tone scale (symmetrical, consecutive whole steps) is most commonly used over dominant 7th chords. Its symmetrical structure means no half steps, and it lacks gravitational pull toward a specific tonic, making it suitable for suspended or floating dominant passages. (Chapter 4, p. 12)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 12: 'The Whole Tone Scale (symetrical, consecutive whole steps) most commonly used over dominant 7th chords.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "major6/9", "function_role": "scale-selection", "narrative": "The major pentatonic scale (diatonic major with the 4th and 7th — the active tones — omitted) creates inversions of a major 6/9 chord when harmonized. Its removal of half steps gives it little gravitational pull toward any key center, making it usable across multiple harmonic contexts depending on application. (Chapter 4, p. 13)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 13: 'The Major Pentatonic Scale (same as diatonic major with the active tones 3rd and 7th left out). When harmonized creates inversions of a Major 6/9 chord, with little gravitational pull toward any key center \"depending on the usage\".'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "scale-selection", "narrative": "The harmonic minor scale can be derived quickly from the already-learned diatonic major patterns by raising the fifth scale step (equivalent to raising the seventh of the relative minor). This minimizes new memorization by building on existing pattern knowledge. (Chapter 3, p. 9)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 3, p. 9: 'the relative harmonic minor scales can be quickly learned by simply sharping the fifth scale step of the diatonic scales, which is the same as sharping the seventh of the relative minor scales.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "scale-selection", "narrative": "The melodic minor scale follows ascending/descending rules (half steps at 2nd/3rd and 7th/8th ascending; reverts to natural minor descending), but this rule is a technicality that may be disregarded in favor of the existing bar harmony. Prioritize harmonic context over rote rule-following. (Chapter 4, p. 12)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 4, p. 12: 'The Relative Melodic Minor Scale (with half steps between the 2nd/3rd and 7th/8th scale steps ascending and reverting back to the natural minor descending. NOTE: The ascending and descending rules here are a technicality, which in the final analysis may be disregarded in favor of the existant bar harmony)'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "picking-mechanics", "narrative": "Use alternate picking exclusively during project lesson sessions — no two consecutive strokes in the same direction. The qualitative standard is dynamic equality: upstrokes must sound as strong as downstrokes. Directional alternation alone is insufficient if the strokes are dynamically unequal. (Chapter 7, p. 19; Chapter 8, p. 19)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 7, p. 19: 'Use Alternate Picking only. No two strokes in the same direction, i.e. strive to make up strokes sound as strong as down strokes.'"}, {"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20-Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 8, p. 19: 'Use Alternate Picking only. No two strokes in the same direction, i.e. strive to make up strokes sound as strong as down strokes.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "picking-mechanics", "narrative": "During Weeks 1–13 of the program, play only continuous, uninterrupted eighth notes with no rests, no phrasing, no hammer-ons, no pull-offs, and no other ornamentation. This constraint isolates picking mechanics as the sole variable under development. (Chapter 7, p. 19)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 7, p. 19: 'Play only eighth notes, continuous and uninterrupted. No rests. No phrasing. No hammer-on's. No pull-offts. No other ornamentation. \"Nothing\" but steady eighth notes.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "proscriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "picking-mechanics", "narrative": "Play legato — hold each note as long as possible. Great attention must be given to holding steady time; never rush or drag the tempo. Note sustain and metronomic steadiness are the two non-negotiable execution quality standards for all project lessons. (Chapter 7, p. 19)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 7, p. 19: 'Play Legato. Hold each note as long as possible. Great attention should be given to holding steady time. Do not rush or drag the tempo.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "legato-technique", "narrative": "Hammer-ons, pull-offs, and glissandi are introduced only in Weeks 15–17 of the program, not before. Their strategic value is that they allow multiple notes per single pick stroke, producing a dramatic increase in apparent speed without increasing picking effort. (Chapter 5, p. 15)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 5, p. 15: 'Review the project lessons as before using (a) hammer-on's (b) pull-off's (c) glissandi (slides). The introduction of these techniques should cause your technique and speed to increase dramatically in that via these devices several notes can be produced with one picking stroke.'"}], "provenance": "extracted", "polarity": "prescriptive"}, {"chord_quality": "any", "function_role": "synchronization-warm-up", "narrative": "Begin every practice session with a 5-minute warm-up playing notes slowly all over the fingerboard — low, high, and medium register. String travel distance varies significantly by register (high-neck notes have much greater travel than low notes) and directly causes left/right-hand synchronization failures if not addressed at the start of each session. (Chapter 6, p. 16)", "source_work_id": "jazz-guitar-technique-in-20-weeks", "references": [{"source": "Roberts, Howard - Jazz Guitar Technique in 20 Weeks", "citation": "Chapter 6, p. 16: 'At the beginning of each practice session, warm up for 5 minutes by playing notes all over the fingerboard. Play very slowly, low, high, and medium pitches, to develop a feel for string travel at a given picking area.
